title: Chapter 9: The Prideful 4
content:
Chapter 9

Over at the ancient burial grounds, Lan Sizhui and his companions had turned up nothing of use. Empty-handed, they pivoted to the Goddess Temple, hoping to track down fresh leads.

Tucked into Dafan Mountain alongside generations of ancestral graves from Buddha's Foot Town was a solitary stone shrine. The deity enthroned inside wasn’t the Buddha, nor was it Guanyin. It was consecrated to the Dancing Goddess.

Centuries ago, a local hunter tracking game into the deep ridges stumbled across a bizarre stone outcrop within a natural grotto. Standing nearly ten feet tall, sculpted entirely by the elements, it bore an uncanny likeness to a human form—complete with limbs arranged in an elegant, frozen dance. Stranger still, the contours of a face were faintly discernible on the head, fixed in a serene, smiling gaze.

The townsfolk were mesmerized. They took it for a sacred stone blessed by heaven and earth, immediately spinning lavish myths to explain its existence: an immortal lord pining for the Mystical Goddess of the Nine Heavens, carving her likeness to soothe his lovesickness only to abandon it half-finished when she discovered his insolence; or perhaps the Jade Emperor’s beloved daughter, dead in her youth, her father’s grief crystallizing into stone. The folklore grew colorful, wild, and rampant. Passed from mouth to mouth, the tales eventually convinced even the storytellers themselves. Before long, someone had converted the cave into a shrine, carved the outcrop into a pedestal, named the icon the "Venerable Dancing Goddess," and kept incense burning before it year-round.

Inside, the cavern was cavernous enough to match a two-courtyard temple, with the stone goddess holding court dead center. At a passing glance, it truly was a spitting image of a living woman, down to the fluid grace of her sculpted waist. Seen up close, the texture turned rough and unpolished, yet for raw mother nature to produce a mimicry this eerily human was enough to leave visitors clicking their tongues in awe.

Lan Jingyi swept his Compass of Evil up, down, and around, but the needle remained stubbornly paralyzed. Scraps of guttered candles littered the altar beneath a thick drift of ash, while fruit left in the offering bowls fermented into a sickly sweet rot. Possessing the squeamishness inherent to every Gusu Lan disciple, he fanned the foul air away from his face. "The locals swear wishes made at this temple always come true, so why let it fall into this kind of ruin? Couldn't they hire a few hands to sweep the dust?"

"Seven people have lost their souls in a row," Lan Sizhui countered softly. "Rumors are flying that thunderbolts broke open the old cemetery to loose some ancient fiend. Nobody dares climb this peak anymore. With the incense burning out, there’s naturally nobody left to sweep the floor."

A sneer drifted in from the mouth of the cavern. "A jagged hunk of rock crowned as a deity by god knows who, yet it dares sit here soaking up incense and prostrations!"

Jin Ling strolled inside, hands clasped behind his back. The Silence Spell didn't have a long shelf life, and his jaws had already unlocked. Predictably, the second his mouth opened, nothing civil came out. Looking up at the statue with contempt, he scoffed, "These ignorant bumpkins. The moment trouble knocks, they don’t lift a finger to help themselves—they just waste their days burning incense, bowing to statues, and begging for miracles. The world has millions of mortals; the gods can barely manage their own business, so why would they give a damn about this backwater? Especially when it's an unrecognized, illegitimate wild deity! If this stone is really that omnipotent, fine: I wish for the soul-consuming abomination haunting Dafan Mountain to drop dead in front of my eyes this very second. Think it can deliver?"

A pack of rogue cultivators from minor clans had trailed him inside. Hearing the young master's boast, they instantly buttered him up, barking sycophantic laughter. The quiet grotto became deafening in a heartbeat, choked by the crush of bodies. Lan Sizhui shook his head in quiet disapproval. Turning to leave, his eyes brushed against the statue's features—a soft, blurry face set in a look of merciful benevolence.

Yet looking at it, an odd familiarity nagged at the back of his brain, as if he’d seen that very smile somewhere before.

Where had he seen it?

Sizhui had a gut feeling that this detail was vital. Drawn forward despite himself, he approached the altar, leaning close to examine the features in the gloom. Right at that second, someone stumbled against his shoulder.

A cultivator standing directly behind him collapsed, hitting the stone floor without a whisper of sound. The cavern erupted in shouts, men jumping back on guard. Jin Ling's hand snapped to his hilt. "What's wrong with him?!"

Lan Sizhui dropped to one knee, sword drawn as he checked the fallen man. His breathing was steady and calm, as if he had merely drifted off to sleep, yet no amount of shaking or shouting could bring him around. Sizhui stood up slowly. "It looks as though he's—"

Before the word could leave his tongue, the dark grotto abruptly caught fire with a crimson flare. Blood-red light flooded the walls like a torrential red cataract spilling over stone. Across the altars and shadowy niches, every scrap of candle and incense stick ignited all by itself.

Clang!Swords were wrenched from their sheaths; talismans crackled between tensed fingers. In that split second, a figure charged through the cavern entrance carrying a gourd of medicinal liquor, dousing the Dancing Goddess in a fragrant spray. The air went thick and suffocating with alcohol fumes. Whipping a talisman through the air, the intruder struck a spark and hurled it at the statue. The altar detonated into a towering wall of white-hot fire, turning midnight into blazing noon!

Wei Wuxian tossed the empty Qiankun bag aside, having burnt through every scrap inside. "Clear out!" he hollered. "Get back! Watch out for that Soul-Consuming Goddess!"

Someone shrieked from the crowd: "The statue! Her stance changed!"

A breath earlier, the stone figure had stood with both arms poised high, one hand pointing toward the heavens, one foot raised in a supple, curving dance. Now, silhouetted against the roaring yellow flames, her limbs had dropped completely flat to her sides. There was no mistaking it—nobody’s eyes were playing tricks!

The next second, the stone raised a foot and took a step straight out of the fire!

Wei Wuxian roared, "Run, run, run! Stop swinging your steel! It's useless!"

Most of the cultivators tuned him out completely. Having scoured the woods endlessly for the soul-eating quarry, here it was dropping right into their laps; who was going to walk away from that glory? Yet as a hail of swords, talismans, and prized relics struck the rock, the onslaught failed to slow its stride by an inch. Standing nearly ten feet tall, it moved like a hulking colossus, radiating suffocating malice. Lunging down, it snatched two cultivators, hauling them up to its face. The jagged stone lips seemed to part and snap together.Clatter.Their swords slipped from limp fingers and their heads rolled slack—their souls had been drained dry in a single bite.

Realizing their martial arts were useless against it, the mob finally took Wei Wuxian's advice to heart, stampeding out the entrance and scattering into the timber for dear life. In the screaming confusion, Wei Wuxian scanned the chaotic clearing, his anxiety mounting as Jin Ling remained nowhere in sight. Kicking his mount through the brush, he veered down a bamboo grove, slamming face-first into the retreating Lan disciples.

He waved frantically: "Children!"

Lan Jingyi bristled, "Who are you calling children?! Do you even know what clan we're from? You think scrubbing your face lets you talk down to your elders?!"

Wei Wuxian waved a dismissive hand. "Fine, fine, big brothers! Loose a flare! Call down that… that Hanguang-jun of yours!"

The disciples nodded in a rush, digging into their robes as they jogged. After an awkward pause, Lan Sizhui looked up, pale. "The signal fireworks… we used the last one back at Mo Village."

Wei Wuxian gaped. "You didn't restock?!"

Signal flares weren't the sort of consumable you burned through every day. Sizhui ducked his head, thoroughly mortified. "We forgot."

Wei Wuxian leaned down from the donkey, scowling. "You forgotthat? Wait until your Hanguang-jun hears about this—he'll have your hides!"

Lan Jingyi went ash-gray. "We’re dead. Hanguang-jun is going to skin us alive with clan punishments..."

Wei Wuxian scoffed, "Good! You deserve every cane stroke! A little discipline might actually jog your memory. Now move!"

Lan Sizhui fell into step beside the trotting beast. "Young Master Mo, how did you know? How did you realize it wasn't a soul-eating beast or a soul-consuming phantom, but that stone statue?"

Eyes scouring the shadows for a flash of gold robes, Wei Wuxian answered, "How did I know? I have eyes, don't I?"

Lan Jingyi drew up on the other flank, sandwiching the donkey between them. "Saw what? We looked around plenty too!"

"You looked, but did you use your head? What was lingering around that old graveyard?"

"What else? Dead souls!"

"Exactly—dead souls! Which means it couldn't possibly be a beast or a phantom! Think about it: if it were either of those, with an entire field of dead souls drifting out in the open like a free buffet, why wouldn't it dig in? It wouldn't pass them up."

A chorus of young voices pressed in: "Why not?"

"You kids from Gusu..." Wei Wuxian exhaled, rubbing his temple. "If your sect spent less time forcing you to memorize endless clan genealogies and boring historical trivia, and actually taught you practical field survival, we wouldn't be having this conversation! What is there to not understand? Consuming a dead soul is infinitely easier than ripping out a living one. A mortal's physical body is a shield; extracting their living spirit means having to tear through that barrier first. It’s like..." He glanced down at the huffing, eye-rolling donkey beneath him. "It’s like setting one apple on a table in front of you, and locking a second apple inside an iron chest. Which one do you eat? The one on the table, obviously! This thing strictly huntslivingsouls, and it has the chops to crack them open. It’s picky, and it’s insanely powerful."

Jingyi blinked, wide-eyed. "Wait... that actually makes a ton of sense! Hold on, so you're not actually crazy?!"

Lan Sizhui ran alongside, piecing the logic together aloud. "We all assumed the mudslide and the lightning striking the coffins unleashed the malice, so we naturally blamed a soul-consuming phantom."

"Dead wrong," Wei Wuxian clipped.

"What part is wrong?"

"The chronology and the causality. Let me ask you: between the mudslide and the soul snatching, which came first? Which was the cause, and which was the effect?"

Lan Sizhui answered without missing a beat: "The landslide happened first, followed by the souls being stolen. Cause, then effect."

"Completely backwards. The soul was taken first; the landslide was the aftermath! Eating the soul was the cause; the collapse of the hill was the consequence! The night the slope gave way, a storm blew in and lightning blasted a coffin open—commit that detail to memory. Now, who was the first victim? That lazy deadbeat who got stranded up here overnight. A few days after limping home, he turned around and threw an extravagant wedding."

Lan Jingyi frowned. "What's suspicious about that?"

"Whatisn'tsuspicious about it?! A penniless degenerate who spends his life loafing around suddenly has the coin to fund a lavish, formal marriage ceremony?!"

The boys went quiet. Coming from the Lan clan, generational poverty wasn't exactly a topic on their daily radar.

Wei Wuxian pressed on: "Did any of you take a good look at the dead spirits wandering this peak? There’s an old man who had his skull caved in, wearing burial shrouds stitched from the finest silk. A corpse buried in clothes that rich didn't go into the dirt with empty pockets; his casket would've been packed with precious funerary jade and grave goods. The coffin blasted apart by that storm was almost certainly his, yet the relatives who recovered the bones never found a single scrap of gold. The deadbeat pocketed the lot—that's the only way to explain his overnight fortune. He made his stash the exact night he was trapped on this peak, which means something extraordinary went down while the rain was falling. Caught in a violent squall, where on this mountain could he take shelter? The Goddess Temple. And what is the one thing a desperate commoner does when they step inside a holy shrine?"

Lan Sizhui’s eyes widened. "Make a wish?"

"Bingo. He begged for a stroke of miraculous luck—to strike it rich, get a wife, whatever. And the Goddess granted it: she summoned a bolt of lightning, split the tomb wide open, and set the buried treasure right before his greedy eyes. The transaction was complete. So, on his wedding night, the Goddess dropped in to collect her fee—and drained his soul dry."

Lan Jingyi squinted. "You're just guessing!"

"Of course it's an educated guess! But follow the thread, and suddenly every single bizarre incident makes sense."

Lan Sizhui leaned in. "Then what about Lady A-Yan?"

"Smart question. You probably asked around town before making the climb: A-Yan had just gotten betrothed. What is the one thing every newly engaged girl wishes for?"

Lan Jingyi furrowed his brow. "What kind of wish?"

"Something along the lines of:'I pray my husband loves only me, cherishing me for the rest of his life.'Standard fairy tale."

The boys were thoroughly lost. "Can a wish like that even be granted...?"

Wei Wuxian gestured loosely. "It's simple. Cut her husband’s life short the very next morning, and he technically loved her for the remainder of his days, didn't he?"

The realization hit Jingyi like a splash of cold water. "Oh! Oh, gods! So the day after her engagement, her fiancé was slaughtered by wolves because she’d climbed up to the shrine the evening before and made that exact wish!"

Wei Wuxian drove the point home: "Whether wolves killed him or something else did is up for debate. But notice the anomaly with A-Yan: why was she the only victim whose soul returned? What made her special? She had a living relative who lost his soul immediately after her. Or to put it accurately: someone swapped places with her! Blacksmith Zheng was her father. Watching his precious daughter turn into a hollow shell while physicians threw their hands up in despair, what was a doting father left to do?"

This time, Sizhui caught the rhythm instantly: "He had to rely on a miracle. So he climbed up to the Goddess Temple and wished for his daughter’s soul to be restored!"

"Gold star," Wei Wuxian praised. "That's why A-Yan’s soul was spat back out, and why her father became victim number three. But having a soul ripped away and shoved back in leaves scars; her spirit came back warped. Ever since she woke up, she’s been compulsively mimicking the Goddess's dance and that sickening smile."

The thread tying every victim together was simple: they had made a pact before the altar. And the price for a miracle was their soul.

Originally, the statue had been nothing more than an odd hunk of cliffside rock that happened to mimic a human silhouette. After centuries of soaking in mortal incense and prayers, it developed a spark of spiritual sentience. But twisted by greed, it strayed off the path, turning to consuming human souls to rapidly inflate its spiritual power. Taking souls through granted wishes meant the victims were essentially surrendering their spirits under a mutual, voluntary contract. It mimicked the natural order of karmic exchange; thus, Compasses of Evil wouldn't spin, Spirit Attraction Flags couldn't bait it, and spiritual swords and charms bounced off its skin. The threat stalking Dafan Mountain wasn't a monster or an evil spirit—it was a god. A wild, illegitimate deity forged from centuries of mortal worship! Trying to purge it with standard exorcism tools was like trying to put out an oil fire with more grease!

Lan Jingyi raised a frantic point: "Wait! That man back in the cave lost his soul right before our eyes, but none of us heard him make a wish!"

Wei Wuxian’s heart seized. He yanked the donkey's tether to a halt. "Someone was drained inside the shrine? Tell me what happened—every single word!"

Lan Sizhui ran through the sequence with crisp efficiency. The moment he reached Jin Ling’s mocking boast—“If this stone is really that omnipotent, fine: I wish for the soul-consuming abomination haunting Dafan Mountain to drop dead in front of my eyes this very second”—Wei Wuxian cut in: "How is that not a wish?! That's a textbook invocation!"

The cultivators trailing the boy had laughed along in agreement, binding themselves to the terms. Since the Soul-Consuming Goddess had indeed manifested right in front of them, the contract was fulfilled. Naturally, she was here to collect her invoice!

Suddenly, the donkey dug in its hooves, wheeled around, and sprinted in the opposite direction. Thrown off balance, Wei Wuxian tumbled to the dirt, clinging desperately to the lead rope. From the brush ahead came a sickening crunch of gnashing bone and wet swallowing. A hulking silhouette was hunched over the weeds, its oversized stone head buried in the stomach of a fallen cultivator. At the sound of their approach, the head snapped up, fixing them with a direct stare.

The once-vague features of the stone statue had sharpened. Having gorged on the spiritual cores of several cultivators, its face was now clearly defined—the radiant, smiling face of a woman, blood dripping from her lips as she gnawed on a torn human arm.

The group didn't hesitate; they matched the donkey’s stride and bolted back down the trail.

Lan Sizhui cried out, on the verge of tears, "This makes no sense! The Yiling Laozu wrote that high-tier entities consume souls, while bottom-feeders eat flesh!"

Wei Wuxian sighed in exasperation. "Why are you treating his notes like scripture?! Half the stuff he came up with was a total disaster! Rules evolve! Think of it like a baby: when you don't have teeth, you stick to warm broth, but the second you grow chompers, of course you want to sink them into meat! Her power just spiked, so she’s treating herself to a fresh meal!"

Behind them, the statue hauled itself upright. Towering like a titan, it bounded forward on all fours, thrashing its limbs in a manic, joyful victory dance. Out of nowhere, an arrow whistled through the night, driving straight through her forehead and bursting out the back of her stone skull.

Hearing the twang of the bowstring, Wei Wuxian looked up. Jin Ling was perched on a high ridge, already knocking a second arrow. Drawing the bow to full cheek, he let fly. Another armor-piercing shot caved through the rock, the raw kinetic force stumbling the stone goddess back several paces.

Lan Sizhui cupped his hands, shouting, "Young Master Jin! Fire your flare!"

Jin Ling ignored him completely, dead-set on bagging the prize. With a stony grimace, he laid three arrows across the string at once. Taking two arrows through the head hadn't fazed the statue in the slightest; that serene smile never faltered as she closed the distance toward the ridge. Though her movements looked like a loose, swaying dance, her ground speed was terrifying, eating up the gap in seconds. A few scattered cultivators lunged in from the flanks, attempting to trip her up. Jin Ling’s arrows struck true with every breath, retreating step by step, clearly determined to empty his quiver before drawing steel for close-quarters combat. His form was steady and his aim was lethal, but mortal steel and standard spiritual arrows were useless against a divinity!

Both Jiang Cheng and Lan Wangji were lingering down in Buddha's Foot Town waiting for reports; there was no telling when they’d catch wind of the disaster and hike up. Fire needed water to quench it; if orthodox cultivation tools couldn't touch this thing, he’d have to fight crooked with crooked!

Stepping into Lan Sizhui's blind spot, Wei Wuxian slipped the sword from the boy’s scabbard, hacked down a length of fresh green bamboo, and carved a crude flute in a flurry of flying splinters. Raising the hollow shoot to his lips, he drew in a deep breath.

A piercing, shrieking note tore through the canopy like a war whistle, splitting the dark night and shooting straight for the clouds.

Under ordinary circumstances, he would never have resorted to this. But with his back against the wall, he didn't care what crawled out of the earth—so long as it possessed enough venom and malice to tear this stone goddess to shreds!

Lan Sizhui froze, thoroughly bewildered. Lan Jingyi clamped his hands over his ears, yelling, "Are you serious right now?! Why are you playing a flute at a time like this?! It sounds horrific!"

In the clearing, three more cultivators fell limp, their souls drained. Jin Ling ripped his sword from its scabbard, the creature bearing down less than twenty paces away. His heart hammered violently against his ribs, adrenaline roaring through his ears:If this strike doesn't take her head off, I'm a dead man—so be it!

Right at that second, a metallic clatter rose through the timber of Dafan Mountain.

Clink. Clank.

Slow, then frantic. Halting, then sharp. It echoed through the dead stillness of the timber like heavy iron links striking stone, dragging chains through the undergrowth. Louder, closer, encroaching fast.

The sound carried an unnerving, suffocating aura of slaughter. Even the Dancing Goddess froze, arms frozen mid-dance as she turned her stone head toward the deep, suffocating dark.

Wei Wuxian lowered the bamboo flute, eyes narrowing into the shadows.

Though a heavy sense of dread knotted in his gut, whatever was answering his call was at least willing to take orders.

The clanking snapped to an abrupt halt. A figure stepped out from the pitch-black woods.

Taking in the shape and the face of the arrival, the cultivators' expressions twisted into pure, unadulterated horror.

Even when staring down a monstrous entity capable of swallowing their living souls, these men hadn't broken. Yet the cry that ripped from their throats right now was choked with primal, bone-deep terror.

"…The Ghost General! It's the Ghost General—it's Wen Ning!"

The title was just as notorious as the Yiling Laozu himself; historically, the two names were spoken in the exact same breath.

It referred to only one creature: the premier butcher under Wei Ying’s command, the hound who had unleashed terror and overturned heaven and earth—the fierce corpse whose very bones should have been scattered to dust years ago:

Wen Ning!
